about.lead: I'm Shijie Xie. I build coding agents at MiniMax, then use them to ship my own work. Been through every shift in AI coding: prompts, context, harness. This site keeps my public work and the notes from each.

care.title: What I keep coming back to
paragraphs: How developers can get more done has run through every job I've had. From developer productivity to code intelligence to AI coding, the tools changed, and so did the calls I had to make.
These days I care most about three things: how an agent gets the right context, how its results get checked, and how mistakes surface while it's still running instead of after it says it's done.

agentLord.figureAlt: Two independent review tasks in the Observer, with their session list and execution timeline
agentLord.figureCaption: Observer interface demo · synthetic data, showing how tasks and their execution records are organized. Click for the full-size image.
useParagraphs: You're driving a task from a main session and want other coding agents to review it independently, try a different approach, or pick up where an earlier task stopped. Agent Lord saves each task's session, execution settings and results, so the main session can assign work, follow its progress and collect the output.

It has three parts: a Skill that guides the main session, a CLI runtime that runs and records the work, and an Observer that shows progress. The main session still owns the plan: roles, dependencies, dispatch and acceptance.
agentLord.pipelinesIntro: Start with a single task, or pick a built-in pipeline. A pipeline sets who does the work, what can run in parallel, which evidence unlocks the next stage, and when to stop. The main session that started it moves it forward.
agentLord.pipelinesNote: The pipelines publish pull requests but never merge them. A run that finished, tests that passed and a change that is correct are three separate findings.

capabilities.title: Sessions carry over
capabilities.text: Each task keeps its endpoint and execution settings, so a later turn continues the same task.

capabilities.title: Work is supervised
capabilities.text: Checkpoints follow progress, catch recoverable errors and use the recovery each endpoint supports.

capabilities.title: Every step is recorded
capabilities.text: See the requests, tool activity, results and whatever model evidence the endpoint reports.

capabilities.title: Delivery is checked separately
capabilities.text: Declared files must exist and be non-empty; declared commits and worktrees must meet the delivery conditions.

startParagraphs: You need Node.js 24+, pnpm 9.12.0, Git, and an installed, logged-in CLI for each provider you want to use. It supports Claude Code, Codex CLI and MCode CLI (0.4.9 or later); Codex App tasks also need the host tools in Codex Desktop.
The pipelines rely on three Skills from dev-skills: review-rules, plan-for-agents and explain-as-fool. The README walks through installing them, building the runtime and running a first task.
limitsParagraphs: The Observer doesn't dispatch prompts or move pipelines forward. When you ask, it can open a saved CLI session in a terminal. Codex App endpoints show task state only; CLI endpoints also show conversation and tool activity.

The Skill starts new CLI tasks with permission bypass enabled. "Review only, don't change anything" is an instruction in the task, not a read-only sandbox. Read the execution contract before your first dispatch, and pick the working directory and permissions with care.
agentLord.platformNote: Validated locally on macOS; CI runs on macOS and Linux. Windows isn't claimed as validated end to end.
statusParagraphsHtml: I wrote Agent Lord in August, betting that more agents working at once would get more done. One eight-module job took 14 hours, and for about 76% of that time only one CLI was working. The modules formed a chain, and a downstream module couldn't see what its upstream had just written.

From late September I stopped sending new features through it. They now go through dev-skills: an app the agent can drive, one agent that delivers the feature end to end and proves it works, and a model from another family that checks the result. The repository and its pipelines stay public.

devSkills.workflowIntro: Four stages. You answer the questions at the start, confirm spec.md and verify.md once, and read the decision list before you merge. Everything in between is the agent's job.

stages.name: A. Repository readiness
stages.agent: Makes the app startable, drivable and observable from a worktree: control commands for every entry point, feature maps with numbered criteria, scenario scripts and a smoke set.
stages.you: Answer what the repository can't tell it. Done once per repository, then extended as needed.

stages.name: B. Definition
stages.agent: Asks in rounds and writes a decision summary; turns it into spec.md and verify.md, has another model family check them clause by clause, then freezes them on a feature branch with a draft PR.
stages.you: Answer the questions, confirm the decision summary, then confirm spec and verify once.

stages.name: C. Delivery
stages.agent: One owner implements milestone by milestone and runs the scenarios in the app. Another family verifies the final code independently. The owner handles CI and review until the PR is mergeable, and lists its decisions at the top.
stages.you: Read the decision list, then merge.

stages.name: D. Feedback
stages.agent: Lists the gaps in the repository that this run exposed.
stages.you: Decide which go back into stage A and which into the Skills.

rules.title: Constraints at both ends
rules.text: Definition settles every decision a person has to make and every acceptance requirement. At the end, another model family verifies against verify.md. In between, the owner works on its own and records disagreements instead of stopping.

rules.title: Irreversible operations are yours
rules.text: Merging, force-pushing a shared branch, deleting shared data, sending messages outside, changing a shared environment. The agent finishes everything else, and says why for anything it can't do.

rules.title: Checks go to another model family
rules.text: The gap check of spec and verify, decisions during delivery and the final verification all run in a fresh session of a model from another family.

rules.title: Check results, not process
rules.text: Scripts check two things: spec and verify are the versions you confirmed, and the final code passed verification by another family.

devSkills.catalogIntro: Eleven Skills. The development workflow uses repo-readiness, core-grill, core-spec, deliver, review-rules, mr-for-human and explain-as-fool; the rest work on their own.
requirements: CLIs for models from two different families, installed and logged in. Claude Code and Codex by default; you can also work in MCode, MiniMax's coding agent, and send the checks to whichever CLI runs a different family. With only one family available, the workflow stops at the check instead of checking with the same family.
Node.js 24, git, and gh for GitHub or glab for GitLab.
An app agents can start, operate and observe from a worktree, at the entry points users actually use.
devSkills.installCommands:
claude plugin marketplace add coder-xieshijie/dev-skills
claude plugin install dev-skills@dev-skills
devSkills.basisText: Every rule links back to the OpenAI, Anthropic and Lauren Tan (pstack) sources it rests on. The long version, with the story behind it, is the article.
installParagraphsHtml: MCode, Claude Code and Codex can each install dev-skills as a plugin; you can also clone the repository and link the Skill directories. Use one or the other, not both, or every Skill shows up twice.
Plugin Skills are namespaced: /dev-skills:core-grill in MCode and Claude Code, $dev-skills:core-grill in Codex. Linked from a clone, they have no namespace.
runStepsHtml: Once per repository: /dev-skills:repo-readiness The next requirement is <link or text>.
/dev-skills:core-grill The requirement is <link or text>. Answer the questions and confirm the decision summary.
In the same session: /dev-skills:core-spec Write spec.md and verify.md from the decision summary. Read the gap check and confirm. It freezes both files and opens a draft PR.
In a new session: /dev-skills:deliver Take over <draft PR link>. When it says the PR can be merged, read the decision list at the top, then merge.

projects.name: dev-skills
projects.summary: Agent Skills that take a requirement to a verified, mergeable pull request.
projects.detail: You settle the decisions at the start and read the agent's decisions before you merge. In between, one agent builds the feature and proves it in the running app, and a model from another family checks it.

catalog.name: repo-readiness
catalog.title: Make the app drivable
catalog.description: Sets up agent verification in a repository: a project-local verification Skill with isolated control commands, feature maps with numbered criteria, scenario scripts and a structure check in CI.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:repo-readiness The next requirement is <link or text>

catalog.name: core-grill
catalog.title: Settle the decisions
catalog.description: At the start of a requirement, asks in rounds about the decisions that change what users see, records terms, and hands a confirmed decision summary to core-spec.

catalog.name: core-spec
catalog.title: Write down the contract
catalog.description: Turns the discussion into spec.md (decisions and constraints) and verify.md (acceptance requirements), has another model family check them for gaps, and freezes them after one confirmation.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:core-spec Write spec.md and verify.md from the decision summary

catalog.name: deliver
catalog.title: Deliver and prove it
catalog.description: From the frozen spec and verify, one owner implements, verifies each milestone in the app, gets independent verification from another family, and takes the PR through CI to mergeable.

catalog.name: review-rules
catalog.title: Review with a basis
catalog.description: Criteria for reviewing code and designs, re-checking findings and judging fixes: correctness, minimal change, proportionate complexity, extensibility and clear ownership.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:review-rules Re-check this review comment and give the smallest fix it needs

catalog.name: mr-for-human
catalog.title: Read code an agent wrote
catalog.description: Turns a PR into a reading guide for people: the core decisions first, then the design, the execution logic and where to find the code.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:mr-for-human Walk me through this PR, from the design to the source

catalog.name: explain-as-fool
catalog.title: Explain it plainly
catalog.description: Explains a topic from the basics to someone who knows nothing about it. Other Skills reuse its writing rules.

catalog.name: design-for-review
catalog.title: A design people can review
catalog.description: Turns requirements and design material into a self-contained technical review document.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:design-for-review Turn the confirmed design into a review document

catalog.name: plan-for-agents
catalog.title: A plan agents can run
catalog.description: Creates, revises or checks a complete plan for agents to execute, from requirements and confirmed decisions to steps, outputs and acceptance evidence.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:plan-for-agents Write a complete plan from the confirmed spec

catalog.name: agent-prompt-rules
catalog.title: Prompts with sources
catalog.description: Rules for writing and reviewing prompts for agents, multi-agent pipelines and SKILL.md files, each linked to Anthropic and OpenAI sources.

catalog.name: recon-to-contract
catalog.title: From comparison to contract
catalog.description: Turns a comparison of two or more external references into one executable contract with evidence, decisions and acceptance criteria.
catalog.example: /dev-skills:recon-to-contract Turn this comparison into a migration contract

projects.name: Agent Lord
projects.summary: Coordinate coding agents from one conversation, with repeatable pipelines and verifiable delivery.
projects.detail: Hand work from a Codex, Claude Code or MCode session to Claude Code, Codex CLI, MCode CLI or Codex App tasks. Agent Lord keeps each task's settings, session, progress and output, so the main session can supervise it and continue it later.
projects.updateNote: Agent Lord · now the starting point, not the main workflow

workflows.name: Cross-review
workflows.description: Two reviewers from different model families review the same change on their own, then challenge each other's findings. A fresh session gives its own verdict on every candidate, including the ones they dropped.

workflows.name: Plan cross-review
workflows.description: Two reviewers check a plan against the spec and the current source. A fresh checker settles their findings and rewrites the complete plan; a separate fresh session verifies it against the sources.

workflows.name: Plan to implement
workflows.description: Acceptance scenarios are fixed before any code. One session per plan stage implements on the delivery branch; a reviewer and an acceptance tester then check the same head. With your authorization it opens or updates the PR, and it never merges it.

articles.title: I stopped babysitting my coding agents. Here's the workflow.
articles.summary: One eight-module job took 14 hours, and for about 76% of it only one CLI was working. What I learned from OpenAI, Anthropic and Lauren Tan, and the workflow and three skills I use now.

contributions.title: A slowdown, or a noisy machine?
contributions.summary: Paired re-runs in performance CI, to tell a real regression apart from runner noise and from too little evidence.
contributions.detail: The performance budgets stay the same. Routine checks warn on persistent noise; the full performance check still needs a clear result.
contributions.updateNote: MiniMax Code · performance CI fix merged (PR #280)
